title: Why Is AI So Popular in China?
gist: Foreign Policy's China Brief argues AI is far more publicly trusted in China (87%) than in the U.S. (32%) because Beijing frames it as a manageable bureaucratic/cybernetic tool rather than Silicon Valley's 'winner-takes-all' superintelligence race, a divergence set to shape the agenda of the coming Trump-Xi summit and reflected in new Chinese exit-ban and offshore-trust rules.

themes.theme: Why AI is popular in China but divisive in the U.S.

insights.claim: A poll published in November found 87 percent of people in China say they trust AI, compared with 32 percent in the United States — a divergence the author calls not inevitable, since other technologies like genetically modified crops remain unpopular in China even with government promotion.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: A striking, quantified public-trust gap that helps explain differing regulatory and adoption trajectories for AI in the two largest AI markets, relevant to forecasting consumer AI adoption rates and political backlash risk in each country.
insights.quote: A poll published last November found that 87 percent of people in China say they trust AI, compared with 32 percent in the United States.
insights.locator: The issue reflects how ideological and socially divisive

insights.claim: China situates AI within a long tradition of cybernetics — the study of circular flows and self-adjustment within systems — treating the technology as a vital future capability requiring careful bureaucratic management and public education, in contrast to the U.S. debate, which the author says is driven by Silicon Valley's 'millenarian fantasies about superintelligence.'
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Provides an interpretive framework for why Chinese AI policy reads as more incremental/bureaucratic while U.S. AI discourse is more apocalyptic/winner-take-all — relevant to comparing regulatory philosophy and investment narrative style between the two ecosystems.
insights.quote: China’s approach to AI situates the technology within a long tradition of cybernetics ... treating AI as a vital future technology requiring careful management and public education.
insights.locator: China’s approach to AI situates the technology

insights.claim: At the geopolitical level, the U.S. framing of AI as an existential race translates into a belief in a winner-takes-all AI competition, whereas China's more sober approach treats it as a long-running process of technological progress and exchange.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Frames a key asymmetry in strategic mindset between the two AI superpowers that could affect how each negotiates AI-related issues, including at the coming Trump-Xi summit.
insights.quote: At the geopolitical level, this translates into a belief in a winner-takes-all AI race rather than a long-running process of technological progress and exchange.
insights.locator: The contrast with the AI debate

insights.claim: China's archetypal AI thinker, Kai-Fu Lee, presents a polished, technocratic public image, while more outspoken figures in China's tech industry were cowed by the government's 2020-21 crackdown on the sector — contrasting with U.S. tech leaders described as billionaires increasingly detached from reality and obsessed with AI and apocalyptic scenarios.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Explains why Chinese AI public discourse is comparatively muted and technocratic, a residual effect of the 2020-21 tech crackdown still shaping industry messaging discipline.
insights.quote: More outspoken figures in China’s technology industry were cowed by the government’s crackdown on the sector from 2020-21.
insights.locator: U.S. tech leaders are largely billionaires

insights.claim: China's science-fiction tradition has more often explored interactions between humanlike robots and ordinary people and related ethical questions, whereas American science fiction has fixated on technological singularity — a divergence the author says shapes how leaders in each country think about AI.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: A cultural-narrative explanation for differing elite mental models of AI risk between the U.S. and China, useful context for interpreting each government's regulatory instincts.
insights.quote: Whereas American writing has fixated on technological singularity, Chinese stories have more often explored interactions between humanlike robots and ordinary people as well as the ethical questions that those encounters raise.
insights.locator: The divergence stems in part from

insights.claim: China's digital ecosystem (apps, fintech, and other digital life) has integrated smoothly for most users, while the U.S. digital experience has undergone 'enshittification' — a steady deterioration exemplified by sponsored and deceptive Google search results — making AI simply another well-integrated tool in China versus a further irritant layered onto an already degraded U.S. digital environment.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Suggests underlying digital-platform user experience quality is itself a driver of AI trust/distrust, a factor for assessing AI product adoption friction in the U.S. versus China.
insights.quote: Digital life in the United States, meanwhile, has undergone a long process of “enshittification,” in which the user experience has steadily deteriorated.
insights.locator: Digital life in the United States

insights.claim: At the September Trump-Xi summit, the U.S. delegation will likely focus on maintaining AI superiority and the supposed existential threat of superintelligent computers, while the Chinese delegation will be more concerned with AI's effects on employment, military decision-making, fraud, and maintaining government control over increasingly autonomous systems.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: A forward-looking prediction of the negotiating priorities each side will bring to the September summit, useful for anticipating what AI-related agreements or disagreements might emerge from that meeting.
insights.quote: When Xi visits the United States for a September summit, the U.S. side will likely focus on maintaining AI superiority and on the supposed existential threat posed by superintelligent computers. The Chinese delegation will be more concerned with AI’s effects on employment, military decision-making, and fraud
insights.locator: When Xi visits the United States

insights.claim: U.S. tech leaders and Republican politicians are accusing China of interfering with rising American opposition to AI data centers, including paying local activists, based on what the author calls scant evidence, even though the underlying U.S. opposition to data centers is described as entirely genuine.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Pushes back on a U.S. narrative attributing domestic AI-data-center backlash to Chinese interference, implying investors should treat local opposition to U.S. data-center buildouts as a genuine, durable siting risk rather than a foreign-influence artifact that might dissipate.
insights.quote: Silicon Valley elites and Republican politicians are accusing China of interference, including by paying local activists, based on scant evidence. Though Chinese propaganda might inflame these tensions, the unpopularity of data centers in the United States is entirely genuine.
insights.locator: As public opposition to artificial intelligence

themes.theme: China's tightening tech-security and financial regulation

insights.claim: China's new border-control regulations, taking effect September 15, 2026, will allow foreigners to be officially barred from leaving China for up to five years over technological security concerns, following a precedent set this year when China barred the founders of AI firm Manus from leaving the country amid Meta's attempted acquisition of the company.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: A concrete regulatory risk for foreign employees, investors, or executives involved with Chinese AI companies subject to acquisition or technology-transfer scrutiny — directly relevant to due diligence for any foreign M&A involving Chinese AI firms.
insights.quote: When the rules take effect on Sept. 15, foreigners can officially be prevented from leaving China for up to five years over technological security concerns

insights.claim: The author notes China is no longer merely a perpetrator of tech espionage but is increasingly a target of it as well, as evidenced by the new exit-ban regime designed partly to prevent foreign actors from extracting Chinese technology or personnel.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Signals a shift in China's self-perceived vulnerability profile on technology security, relevant to assessing the trajectory of China's tech-protection regulatory regime.
insights.quote: underscoring the fact that China is no longer a merely perpetuator of tech espionage but increasingly a target as well.
insights.locator: Exit bans are commonly used as a coercive tool

insights.claim: China has issued new rules imposing a 20 percent tax on offshore trusts, shocking wealthy Chinese families who are scrambling to respond, extending Beijing's regulatory reach over Chinese citizens' overseas wealth despite China otherwise being a relatively low-tax environment for individuals.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: A concrete new tax policy (20% on offshore trusts) directly relevant to wealth-management and private-banking clients with Chinese-national beneficiaries or trust structures.
insights.quote: China has issued new rules imposing a 20 percent tax on offshore trusts, shocking wealthy families who are now scrambling to respond.

insights.claim: Like the United States but unlike almost every other country, China taxes its nationals living abroad, though it has historically struggled to enforce this — a gap the new offshore-trust rules are intended to close.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Clarifies that China's global tax-enforcement ambitions are now catching up to its formal legal claims over citizens abroad, relevant to compliance planning for Chinese expatriates and dual nationals.
insights.quote: Like the United States, but unlike almost every other country, China also taxes its nationals living abroad, though it has historically struggled to enforce this.
insights.locator: China is by and large a relatively low-tax environment

insights.claim: New details emerged about a bizarre California killing in which Han Chinese brothers Jianquan Bo and Zhengfeng Bo allegedly kidnapped a Uyghur business associate, Shukur Aikebaer, after a business dispute over a multimillion-dollar apartment complex, and Zhengfeng fatally shot him before being killed by police; the author assesses that despite initial suspicion of a Chinese intelligence operation targeting a Uyghur activist, available details make that explanation unlikely since all three men were in their 60s with a long business relationship and Aikebaer had no apparent political activism.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Illustrates the author's skepticism toward reflexively attributing violent incidents involving Chinese nationals abroad to state intelligence operations, a useful corrective for overreading isolated crime stories as geopolitical signals.
insights.quote: Several people in the U.S. counterintelligence community raised the case to me as a possible Chinese intelligence operation. ... But the available details make that explanation unlikely

insights.claim: Following a prior investigation into a child's death in a Chinese gene-editing trial, Stat News reported a similar case involving boys aged 4-8 with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, with Chinese state media's most authoritative outlets (Xinhua, People's Daily) notably silent, suggesting authorities are still deciding how to handle the scandal.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Flags an unfolding biomedical-ethics scandal in China's gene-editing trials with potential regulatory and reputational implications for the sector, worth monitoring for further disclosures.
insights.quote: Following the recent investigation by Science and Retraction Watch into the death of a child in a Chinese gene-editing trial, Stat News has reported a similar case.
